ee:2003:q1.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 1
ee:2003:q1.question: Figure Shows the waveform of the current passing through an inductor of resistance $1\Omega$ and inductance 2 H. The energy absorbed by the inductor in the first four seconds is

detailed_solution.concept: Electric Circuits - Basics of Electric Circuit
detailed_solution.markdown:
For $0 \lt t \lt 2s$ current varies linearly with time and given as $i(t)=3t$ and for $2s \lt t \lt 4s$ current is constant, $i(t)=6A$.

The energy absorbed by the inductor (Resistance neglected) in the first 2 sec,

$E_L=\int_{0}^{T}Li\frac{di}{dt}=E_{L_1}+E_{L_2}$

$E_{L_1}=\int_{0}^{2}Li \left (\frac{di}{dt} \right )dt$

$\;\;=\int_{0}^{2} 2 \times 3t \times 3\; dt$

$\;\;=18\int_{0}^{2}t\; dt$

$$\;\;=18 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^2}{2} \end{matrix}\right|^2_0$$

$\;\;= 18 \times \left [ \frac{4}{2}-0 \right ]=36J$

The energy absorbed by the inductor in ($2\rightarrow 4$) second

$E_{L_2}=\int_{2}^{4}Li\left ( \frac{di}{dt}dt \right )$

$\;\;=\frac{2}{4}2 \times 6 \times 0 \;dt=0 J$

A pure indictor does not dissipate enegy but only stores it. Due to resistance, some energy is dissipated in the resistor. Therefore, total energy stored in the inductor and the energy dissipated in the resistor.

The energy dissipated by the resistance in 4 sec.

$E_R=\int_{0}^{T}i^2 R\;dt$

$\;\;=\int_{0}^{2}(3t)^2 \times 1 \;dt+\int_{2}^{4}6^2 \times 1 \; dt$

$\;\;=9\int_{0}^{2}t^2\;dt +36\int_{2}^{4}1 \; dt$

$$\;\;=9 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^3}{3} \end{matrix}\right|_0^2+36t|_2^4$$

$\;\;=9 \times \left ( \frac{8}{3} \right )+36 \times 2$

$\;\;=24+72=96J$

The total energy absorbed by the inductor in 4 sec

$=96 J +36 J =132 J$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

detailed_solution.markdown:

$I_P+I_Q+I_C+I_L=0$

$\therefore \;\; V_L=L\left ( \frac{di}{dt} \right )$

$\;\;\;=2 \times 2 \times 8 \sin 2t$

$\;\;\;=32 \sin 2t$

NOTE: KCL is based on the law of conservation of charges.

ee:2003:q8.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 8
ee:2003:q8.question:
A stand alone engine driven synchronous generator is feeding a partly inductive
load. A capacitor is now connected across the load to completely nullify the
inductive current. For this operating condition.
options: the field current and fuel input have to be reduced
the field current and fuel input have to be increased
the field current has to be increased and fuel input left unaltered
the field current has to be reduced and fuel input left unaltered

detailed_solution.markdown: Assuming resistance of the armature to be zero. In first case, the generator is feeding a partly inductive load. It means that generator is supplying lagging power. The generator supplies a lagging power factor current when it is overexcited which is represented by $E_{f_1}$. In second case, a capacitor is connected across the load to completely nullifythe inductive current. It means the generator supplies no reactive power and unity power factor current is drawn from the generator. The excitation ($E_{f_2}$) corresponding to unity power factor is known as normal excitation. From the phasor diagram $E_{f_1} \gt E_{f_2}$ and as the field current approximately directly proportional to excitation, the field current has to be reduced. From phasor diagram $E_{f_1} \sin \delta _1=E_{f_2} \sin \delta _2=\text{constant}$ $P_e(\text{ power delivered})=\frac{E_fV_t}{X_s}\sin \delta$ Fuel input remains unaltered. Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

A control system is defined by the following mathematical relationship

$\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}+6\frac{dx}{dt}+5x=12(1-e^{-2t})$

detailed_solution.concept: Control Systems - Mathematical Models of Physical Systems
detailed_solution.markdown:
Taking (LT) on both sides

$(s^2+6s+5)X(s)=12\left ( \frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+2} \right ) =\frac{24}{s(s+2)}$

$X(s)=\frac{24}{s(s+2)(s+1)(s+5)}$

Responce at $t\rightarrow \infty$

Using final value theorem

$\lim_{t\rightarrow \infty }x(t)=\lim_{s \rightarrow 0}sX(s)$

$=\lim_{s \rightarrow 0}\frac{s \times 24}{s(s+2)(s+1)(s+5)}=2.4$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

ee:2003:q48.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 48
ee:2003:q48.question:
A 3-phase induction motor is driving a constant torque load at rated voltage and frequency. If both voltage and frequency are halved, following statements relate to the new condition if stator resistance, leakage reactance and core loss are ignored

1. The difference between synchronous speed and actual speed remains same
2. The airgap flux remains same
3. The stator current remains same
4. The p.u. slip remains same

Among the above, correct statements are

detailed_solution.concept: Electrical Machines - Three Phase Induction Machines
detailed_solution.markdown:
$$\begin{aligned} V &\propto f\phi \\ &\text{in induction machine}\\ V_2&= \frac{V_1}{2}\\ \text{and}\;\; f_2 &=\frac{f_1}{2} \\ \frac{V_1}{V_2} &=\frac{f_1\phi _1}{f_2\phi _2} \\ \phi _2&= \left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )\left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )\phi _1\\ &= \left ( \frac{V_1/2}{V_1} \right )\left ( \frac{f_1}{f_1/2} \right )\phi _1\\ &= \phi _1 \end{aligned}$$

So, air-gap flux remains same.

$(X_2')_1=$ nominal rotor stanstill reactance referred to stator (at frequency $f_1$)

$$\begin{aligned} (X_2')_2 &= \left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right )(X_2')_1\\ &= \left ( \frac{f_1/2}{f_1} \right )(X_2')_1\\ &= \frac{(X_2')_1}{2}\\ (\omega _s)_2 &= \left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right ) (\omega _s)_1\\ &= \left ( \frac{f_1/2}{f_1} \right ) (\omega _s)_1\\ &=\frac{(\omega _s)_1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Torque developed in induction motor

$T=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2 +{X'_2}^2}$

For normal steady state oprating region, slip is very low

$\frac{R'_2}{s} \gt \gt X'_2$

$T=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2}=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{sV^2}{R'_2}$

As the load torque is constant

$$\begin{aligned} T_1 &=T_2 \\ \frac{s_1V_1^2}{(\omega _s)_1R'_2}&= \frac{s_2V_2^2}{(\omega _s)_2R'_2}\\ \Rightarrow \;\; s_2 &=\frac{(\omega _s)_2}{(\omega _s)_1} \times \left ( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right )^2 s_1\\ &=\frac{(\omega _s)_1/2}{(\omega _s)_1} \times \left ( \frac{V_1}{V_1/2} \right )^2 s_1 \\ s_2 &= \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times s_1=2s_1 \end{aligned}$$

Difference between synchronous speed and actual speed

$$\begin{aligned} \omega _s -\omega _r &= s\omega _s\\ (\omega _s)_1 -(\omega _r)_2 &= s_2(\omega _s)_2\\ &=(2s_1) \times \frac{(\omega _s)_1}{2} =s_1(\omega _s)_1 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the difference between synchronous speed and actual speed remain same.

Stator current

$$\begin{aligned} |I_s| &= \frac{V}{\sqrt{(R'_2/s)^2+{X'}_2^2}} \\ \text{as}\;\; R'_2/s & \gt \gt X'_2 \\ |I_s|&=\frac{sV}{R'_2} \\ |I_{s1}|&= s_1\frac{V_1}{R'_2}\\ |I_{s2}|&=s_2\frac{V_2}{R'_2} \\ ||I_{s2}&=(2s_1)\times \frac{V_1/2}{R'_2}=\frac{s_1V_1}{R'_2} \\ ||I_{s1}&=|I_{s2}| \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, stator current remains same.

Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

ee:2003:q54.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 54

positive sequence impedance of the line based on 100 MVA and 11 kV is j0.2.
The line to line voltage at the load terminals is measured to be less than 11 kV. The total reactive power to be injected at the terminals of the load to increase
the line-to-line voltage at the load terminals to 11 kV is

primary.subtopicLabel: Compensation Techniques and Voltage Profile Control

detailed_solution.concept: Power Systems - Compensation Techniques and Voltage Profile Control
detailed_solution.markdown:
$|V_s|=|V_R|=11kV$

p.u. impedance of the line = j0.2 p.u.

Impedance of the line = p.u. impedance  x Base impedance

$x= j0.2 \times \frac{11^2}{100}=j0.242\Omega$

Active power at receiving end $=P_R=100 MW$

$$\begin{aligned} P_R&=\frac{|V_s||V_R|}{x}\sin \delta \\ 100 &= \frac{11 \times 11}{0.242} \sin \delta \\ \delta &=11.54^{\circ} \end{aligned}$$

Reactive power at receiving end

$$\begin{aligned} Q_R&=\frac{|V_s||V_R|}{x}\cos \delta -\frac{|V_R|^2}{x} \\ &= \frac{11 \times 11}{0.242} \cos 11.54 -\frac{11^2}{0.242} \\ &=-10.1 \text{ MVAR} \end{aligned}$$

Since poer factor =1

Load reactive power should be zero

Therefore, reactive power to be injected at terminals $=-Q_R=-(-10.1)=10.1 \text{ MVAR}$

Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

ee:2003:q56.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 56

ee:2003:q74.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 74
ee:2003:q74.question:
The following equation defines a separately excited dc motor in the form of a differential equation
$\frac{d^{2}\omega }{dt}+\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}+\frac{K^{2}}{LJ}\omega =\frac{K}{LJ}V_{a}$

$$\begin{bmatrix} \frac{d^2\omega}{dt^2}\\ \frac{d\omega}{dt} \end{bmatrix}=P\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{d\omega}{dt}\\ \omega \end{bmatrix}+QV_a$$
where the P matrix is given by

detailed_solution.markdown:
Let, $x_1=\frac{d\omega }{dt}$ and $x_2=\omega$

$\;\;\; \dot{x_2}=x_1$

$$\frac{d^2\omega }{dt^2}+\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}+\frac{k^2}{LJ}\omega =\frac{k}{LJ}V_a$$

$$\frac{d^2\omega }{dt^2}=-\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}-\frac{k^2}{LJ}\omega + \frac{k}{LJ}V_a$$

$\Rightarrow \;\; \dot{x_1}=-\frac{B}{J}x_1-\frac{k^2}{LJ}x_2+\frac{k}{LJ}V_a$

$\;\;\dot{x_2}=x_1$

$$\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x_1}\\ \dot{x_2} \end{bmatrix}=P\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}+QV_a$$

where,

$$P=\begin{bmatrix} -\frac{B}{J} & -\frac{k^2}{LJ}\\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$Q=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{k}{LJ}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

ee:2003:q77.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 77
ee:2003:q77.question: The block diagram of a control system is shown in figure. The transfer function G(s) = Y(s)/U(s) of the system is

detailed_solution.concept: Control Systems - Mathematical Models of Physical Systems
detailed_solution.markdown: Integrator are represented as 1/s in s-domain As per the block diagram, the corresponding signal flow graph is drawn One forward path $P_{1}\, =\, 2/s^{2}$ The individual loops are, $\; \; \; L_{1}\, =\, -\frac{3}{s},\: L_{2}\, =\, -\frac{12}{s} and L_{3}\, =\, -\frac{18}{s^{2}}$ $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are non-touching loops $\; \; \; L_{1}L_{2}\, =\, \frac{36}{s^{2}}$ The loops touches the forward path $\Delta _{1}=1$ The graph determinant is $\; \; \; \Delta \, =\, 1-\left ( L_{1}+L_{2}+L_{3} \right )+L_{1}L_{2}$ $\; \; \; \; =1+\frac{3}{s}+\frac{12}{s}+\frac{18}{s^{2}}+\frac{36}{s^{2}}$ Applying mason's gain formula, $\; \; \; G\left ( s \right )=\frac{Y\left ( s \right )}{U\left ( s \right )}=\frac{P_{1}\Delta _{1}}{\Delta }$ $\; \; \; \; =\frac{2/s^{2}}{1+\frac{3}{s}+\frac{12}{s}+\frac{18}{s^{2}}+\frac{36}{s^{2}}}$ $\; \; \; \; =\frac{2}{s^{2}+15s+54}=\frac{2}{\left ( s+9 \right )\left ( s+6 \right )}$ $\; \; \; \; =\frac{1}{27\left ( 1+\frac{s}{9} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{6} \right )}$ Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

ee:2003:q80.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 80
ee:2003:q80.question:
A wattmeter reads 400 W when its current coil is connected in the R-phase
and its pressure coil is connected between this phase and the neutral of a
symmetrical 3-phase system supplying a balanced star connected 0.8 p.f.
inductive load. This phase sequence is RYB. What will be the reading of this
wattmeter if its pressure coil alone is reconnected between the B and Y phases,
all other connections remaining as before ?

detailed_solution.concept: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Measurement of Energy and Power
detailed_solution.markdown: Taking $V_R$ as the reference and assuming phase to neutral voltage $=V$ $$\begin{aligned} V_R &=V\angle 0^{\circ} \\ V_Y &= V\angle -120^{\circ}\\ and \;\; V_B &=V\angle -240^{\circ} \end{aligned}$$ $$\begin{aligned} V_RI_R \cos \phi &=400 W \\ VI_R \times 0.8&= 400W\\ VI_R&=400\;\;...(i) \\ I_R&=I_R\angle -36.87^{\circ} \end{aligned}$$ [p.f. =0.8 lag, inductive load] $$\begin{aligned} V_{YB} &=V_{YB}-V_B \\ &= V\angle -120^{\circ}- V \angle -240^{\circ}\\ &=\sqrt{3}V\angle -90^{\circ} V\\ I_R&=I_R\angle -36.87^{\circ}A \end{aligned}$$ Angle between $V_{YB}$ and $I_{R}$ $\theta =-90^{\circ}-(-36.87^{\circ})=53.13^{\circ}$ As pressure coil connected between Y and B phase. Reading of wattmeter$=V_{YB}I_R\cos \theta$ From equation (i) $=\sqrt{3}V \times I_R \times \cos (-53.13) =\sqrt{3}\times 500 \times 0.6=519.6W$ Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

ee:2003:q81.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 81
ee:2003:q81.question:
The inductance of a certain moving-iron ammeter is expressed as
L = $10+30 -\frac{\theta ^{2}}{4} \; \mu H$, where  $\theta$ is the deflection in radians from the zero position. The control spring torque is $25 \times 10^{-6}$ Nm/radian. The deflection of the pointer in radian when the meter carries a current of 5 A, is

detailed_solution.concept: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Galvanometers, Voltmeters and Ammeters
detailed_solution.markdown:
Deflection torque in moving-iron ammeter,

$T_d=\frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta }$

Inductance,   $L=\left ( 10+3\theta -\frac{\theta ^2}{4} \right )\mu H$

Rate of change of inductance with deflection

$\frac{dL}{d\theta }=\frac{d}{d\theta }\left ( 10+3\theta -\frac{\theta ^2}{4} \right )$

$\;\;\;=\left ( 3- \frac{\theta }{2}\right )\mu H/rad$

Current , $I=5A$

Deflecting torque,

$$\begin{aligned} T_d &=\frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta } \\ T_d &= \frac{1}{2} \times 5^2 \times \left ( 3-\frac{\theta }{2} \right ) \times 10^{-6}\\ &= \frac{25}{2}\left ( 3-\frac{\theta }{2} \right )\times 10^{-6} Nm \end{aligned}$$

Controlling torque

$T_c=k\theta =25 \times 10^{-6}\theta$

At equilibrium,

$$\begin{aligned} T_c &= T_d\\ 25 \times 10^{-6}\theta &= \frac{25}{2}\left ( 3-\frac{\theta }{2} \right )\times 10^{-6} \\ \frac{5\theta }{2} &= 3\\ \theta &= 1.2 \text{rad} \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

ee:2003:q83.title: GATE EE 2003 | Set 1 | Question: 83

meter is altered so that the phase angle between the applied voltage and the

detailed_solution.markdown:
Measured value $=VI \sin (\Delta -\phi )$

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta &= 80^{\circ}\\ pf&= \cos \phi =1\\ \phi &= 0^{\circ}\\ V&= 220V\\ I&= 5A \\ \text{Error}&=VI \sin (\Delta -\phi )-VI \cos \phi \\ &=220 \times 5 \sin(85-0^{\circ})-220 \times 1 \times 1\\ &\approx -4.2W \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.
